editorial.headline: Research at the Root of Agriculture and Animal Health
editorial.standfirst: A systematic R&D activity spanning agriculture, fisheries, forestry, marine fields and veterinary science, open nationally to full foreign ownership and not blocked by Bali’s stated moratorium.
editorial.body:
At its core, this activity is systematic research and development for the knowledge systems that support agriculture and animal health. It reaches through agricultural science, animal husbandry, forestry, fisheries, marine affairs and veterinary medicine. Its stated scope includes agricultural biotechnology; agricultural, fisheries and forestry sciences; animal and dairy science; veterinary science; fertiliser research; and research into sustainable agricultural development. That breadth spans land- and sea-based sectors as well as the veterinary dimension of animal health. Environmental research is excluded from the activity’s stated remit.

This classification is for businesses undertaking that regular, systematic R&D. Registration is open at small, medium and large scale, putting a modest specialist research operation and a larger research organisation on the same stated footing as to scale. Being small, medium or large speaks to permitted scale, while the defined subject remains the R&D scope itself. The subject does not narrow to one discipline: biotechnology, dairy science, fertiliser work and sustainable agricultural development sit alongside the wider agricultural, forestry, fisheries, marine and veterinary fields. The unifying thread is research conducted regularly enough to be systematic.

For foreign ownership at the national level, the position is direct. The activity is marked TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign participation of 100%. In practical terms, a foreign investor may hold up to 100% of the business carrying out this activity nationally. That is a full foreign-ownership ceiling, not a partial cap, and it belongs to the national position set out for this activity. Bali, however, has its own registration context and must be read on its own terms.

Bali’s separate reading is not a block. The activity is listed as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the record expressly says that it is not blocked by the provincial moratorium. The reason lies in its medium-high or high-risk character: Bali’s permanent, island-wide PMA moratorium blocks Low and Medium-Low risk activities, categories not assigned here. The Bali position should nevertheless be verified for the relevant address, exactly as the record directs. For a foreign-owned registration in Bali, the honest position is clear: the activity is nationally open to up to 100% foreign ownership and is not blocked by the stated moratorium, while address-specific verification remains part of the Bali picture.
